sentences.text: Diamantinasaurus was a medium-sized titanosaurian, a group of large sauropod dinosaurs, measuring 16 meters long and weighing up to 25 tonnes.
This large quadrupedal herbivore moved on four legs and ate plants.
The known fossil material includes almost the entire right forelimb, plus the left humerus and left first metacarpal.
A diagnostic feature of the animal is that the glenoid articulation of the scapula is rotated outward, a trait unique among somphospondylans.
The scapula of Diamantinasaurus is robust with a round cross-section, distinguishing it from other somphospondylans.
A 2023 study described specimen AODF 0906, which preserved a more complete skull estimated at 50 cm in length.
The species D. matildae was first described and named in 2009 by Scott Hocknull and colleagues from fossils found in the Winton Formation.
Specimens AODF 0603 and AODF 0604 were described in 2009 by Scott Hocknull and colleagues.
The genus name combines the Diamantina River with the Greek word for lizard, and the species name references the song "Waltzing Matilda".
The Diamantinasaurus discovery was the largest dinosaur find in Australia since Muttaburrasaurus in 1981.
The skull shape of Diamantinasaurus was more similar to brachiosaurids than to derived titanosaurs, suggesting a close relationship with the Argentinian titanosaur Sarmientosaurus.
Diamantinasaurus possessed at least five, and possibly six, sacral vertebrae.
Fossilized gut contents revealed that Diamantinasaurus engaged in bulk feeding and multi-level browsing, consuming conifers, seed ferns, and flowering plants.
A 2014 study placed Diamantinasaurus as a lithostrotian in a relatively derived position within Titanosauria.
Gorscak & O'Connor (2019) recovered Diamantinasaurus as a saltasaurid using parsimony analysis, but a variable-rates Bayesian analysis placed it just outside Saltasauridae.
Diamantinasaurus lived in Australia during the early Late Cretaceous, approximately 94 million years ago.
Diamantinasaurus lived in the middle Cretaceous, approximately 98 to 95 million years ago (Turonian stage), in what is now Australia.
Diamantinasaurus fossils were recovered from the Winton Formation, dated to approximately 93 million years ago.
The fossils were found in the middle-upper section of the Winton Formation, dating to the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Poropat et al. (2014) hypothesized that the absence of carpal bones in Diamantinasaurus fossils indicates their genuine absence in life, similar to Opisthocoelicaudia and Alamosaurus.
Poropat et al. (2014) suggested based on Diamantinasaurus that all titanosaurs possessed ossified phalanges, a view that contrasts with earlier studies.
A 2011 study described the smallest positively identified titanosaur embryo, which shares the most features with Diamantinasaurus and Rapetosaurus.
